extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of ethics / ancient philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Exegesis and normative claims from Aristotle (Nicomachean Ethics, Books VI–VII) about knowledge, Practical Wisdom (phronesis), virtue, akrasia (imperfect self-control), brutishness, and the object-matter of moral states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue as a state implying Right Reason / Practical Wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue is a 'state' which is accordant with Right Reason and implies the possession of Right Reason (Practical Wisdom) rather than being merely a reasoning process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle revises the Socratic claim that virtues are merely intellectual knowledge: virtues are not identical with reasoning but presuppose Practical Wisdom. The 'state' which is in accordance with Practical Wisdom is Virtue — it implies possession of right reason, not merely conformity with it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Natural Virtue and Matured Virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two forms of moral dispositions: Natural Virtue (present by nature) and Matured Virtue (formed through habituation and requiring Practical Wisdom).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural states (found in children and brutes) are insufficient unless combined with the intellectual element; Matured Virtue cannot be formed without Practical Wisdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual dependence of Practical Wisdom and moral goodness
rubrics_metrics.description: One cannot be strictly good without Practical Wisdom, nor Practically-Wise without moral goodness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle argues that moral choice cannot be right independently of Practical Wisdom and Moral Goodness because Practical Wisdom provides the correct End that guides action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical Wisdom supplies the right End for moral choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical Wisdom (phronesis) supplies the right End (telos) that causes doing those things which conduce to the End; moral choice depends on this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Practical Wisdom gives the right End, moral choice cannot be right independently of it. Practical Wisdom is not a 'master of science' (it does not make use of science) but gives guidance about how to act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge defined as knowing causes; demonstration as source of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: We 'know' things in the strict sense when we know the cause by reason; demonstrative reasoning (a syllogism apt to produce knowledge) is how we obtain such Knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle equates true demonstrative knowledge with having syllogisms whose premises make the conclusion necessary and causal; other kinds of opinion are distinguished from this strict knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for premises of demonstrative knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Premises of demonstration must be true, first (indemonstrable), incapable of syllogistic proof, better known, prior in order of time, and causes of the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle explains 'first' as principles akin to the conclusion; an axiomatic premise is necessary for learning something else. Premises must be better known and prior (either by nature or relative to us) so that they function as causes of the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles must be known better than conclusions and believed infallibly
rubrics_metrics.description: One who attains demonstrative Knowledge must know and believe the principles better than the conclusion and be infallible regarding the contradictories of those principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since principles are causes of our knowing, they should be more firmly believed; Aristotle insists on strong epistemic status for premises to secure demonstrative knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three moral defects to be avoided: Vice, Imperfect Self-Control, Brutishness
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral character has three problematic forms: Vice, Imperfect Self-Control (akrasia), and Brutishness (or morbid states); these have different etiologies and moral statuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle treats these as distinct kinds: Vice is corruption of higher principles, Brutishness is absence of the higher principle (due to nature or disease), and Imperfect Self-Control is a human failing under passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-Control and Endurance as praiseworthy; Imperfect Self-Control and Softness as blameworthy
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-Control (continence) and Endurance (patience) are goods and praiseworthy; their counterparts, Imperfect Self-Control and Softness, are low and blameworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle enumerates common opinions that Self-Control and Endurance are praiseworthy and frames the subsequent enquiry to clarify these characters and their object-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition contrast: man of Self-Control vs man of Imperfect Self-Control
rubrics_metrics.description: The man of Self-Control is apt to abide by his resolution; the man of Imperfect Self-Control is apt to depart from his resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle aligns Self-Control with adherence to resolution (guided by reason) and Imperfect Self-Control with yielding to passions despite convictions; later refinements consider object-matter and relations to reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperfect Self-Control: action at instigation of passions despite knowing wrong
rubrics_metrics.description: Imperfect Self-Control consists in doing things at the instigation of passions while knowing them to be wrong (acting against one's better judgment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle rejects Socrates' claim that such failure is impossible; he analyses senses of 'knowing' and shows how passion can prevent the exercise of knowledge even when the person 'knows' in some senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfected Self-Mastery as union of Self-Control and Endurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfected Self-Mastery (sovereignty over passions) unites Self-Control and Endurance and is sometimes equated with the ideal of complete self-mastery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some say that whoever unites Self-Control and Endurance attains Perfected Self-Mastery; Aristotle treats this as a debated point to be examined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object-matter limitation: bodily pleasures (touch/taste) are proper objects of Self-Control/akrasia
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper object-matter of Self-Control, Imperfect Self-Control, Perfected Self-Mastery, and utter loss of Self-Control consists in pleasures and pains arising from touch and taste (bodily enjoyments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other goods (honour, wealth, victory) can be objects of excessive desire but are treated differently (we add a qualifier, e.g., 'of respect to honour'), so akrasia in the strict sense is restricted to bodily pleasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excesses regarding honour/wealth are blameworthy but named with qualification
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive pursuit of honour, wealth, or similar goods is blameworthy, but such states are not called 'Imperfect Self-Control' simply — they are named 'Imperfect Self-Control with respect to X' by analogy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because these objects are choice-worthy in themselves, their excess is blameworthy without being the same species as bodily akrasia; the naming is analogical (similarity but not identity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical action as a syllogism: universal + particular; failure when the particular is misassessed
rubrics_metrics.description: All action may be analyzed as a practical syllogism: a universal maxim plus a particular (sensory) premiss yields an action; failure of Self-Control occurs when desire distorts or overrides the particular premiss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'All that is sweet should be tasted' (universal) + 'This is sweet' (particular) -> action. Desire can make the particular 'work' despite a contrary universal, producing akratic behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passions put persons in states like drunkenness or sleep: knowledge present but not exercised
rubrics_metrics.description: When under strong passions (anger, lust), people can have the propositions constituting knowledge but fail to exercise them — similar to being drunk, asleep, or mad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle uses this to explain how someone can 'know' in some sense yet act contrary to that knowledge; the minor practical premiss is absent or merely spoken, not truly operative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brutes lack universals and therefore cannot properly be of Imperfect Self-Control
rubrics_metrics.description: Brutes (animals) do not possess the capacity to conceive universals and thus cannot be akratic in the proper sense; analogous states in animals are only metaphorically called 'imperfect self-control'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This supports restricting the proper object-matter and species of akrasia to beings capable of deliberative universals (humans).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction among pleasures: natural, species-specific, and pathological/customary
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures divide into those naturally pleasant (some universal, some species-specific) and those arising from disease, maiming, or custom (pathological tastes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where pleasures are pathological or brutish, the corresponding moral states are Brutish or Morbid, not Imperfect Self-Control in the proper human sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperfect Self-Control with respect to lusts is more disgraceful than with respect to anger
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing in Self-Control due to lusts is judged more disgraceful and unjust than failing through anger because anger 'listens to Reason but mishears it', whereas lust does not follow Reason and is more insidious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle argues anger is more 'open' and in some ways more natural, while lust involves deceit and pleasure without pain; thus akrasia from lust is morally worse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brutishness vs Vice: different moral statuses and sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Brutishness (absence of reason, disease-caused or natural) is not vice in the same sense as human moral vice; it is to be feared because it lacks the highest principle, but its harm differs from a wicked human agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A bad man (vice) can do far more harm than a brute because the moral subject with intellect can originate greater wrongdoing; brutishness is often caused by disease or nature rather than corruption of Reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: The incurability criterion: utter pursuit of excessive pleasures without remorse is incurable
rubrics_metrics.description: One utterly void of Self-Control pursues excessive pleasures and avoids moderate pains not by moral choice but despite moral choice, and if he is incapable of remorse he is incurable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle uses incapacity for remorse as a sign of incurability: moral remediation requires the capacity for remorse and the possibility of being turned by reason.
